assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong, controllable coupling between a single microwave photon and an artificial atom possible on a chip, and it became the architecture for dispersive readout, two-qubit gates and error-correction experiments in superconducting processors. The idea is original, the physics is clear and the impact is lasting across quantum optics, mesoscopic physics and quantum technology. I am close to this field, so I rate its depth with some familiarity but also with a bias that I should acknowledge.
assessment.attribution: Blais (theory proposal with Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf, 2004) plus Wallraff (first strong-coupling experiment, 2004) and Schoelkopf (Yale group, cavity and transmon development) form a credible three-person configuration. Girvin and others made important contributions that cannot be named because they are not credited here, and the transmon and Yale/ETH sharing is not fully resolved.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent groups and a decade-plus of use in processors. The interpretation is stable. The main timing question is whether a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling is advisable; the discoveries are distinct, but the committee would have to weigh this.
uncertainties: Whether recognition so close to the 2025 circuit prize is appropriate.
Credit division among theory proposal, first experiment and later transmon/architecture development; I am relying on memory for the exact history.
My own field proximity may bias my assessment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, followed by the observation in HgTe quantum wells, opened the field of topological phases protected by time-reversal symmetry. The concept is original, clean and has had large reach into materials, spintronics and quantum matter. This is the strongest of the topological-insulator candidates and has the clearest theory-experiment pair.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical predictions (graphene QSH and the Z2 invariant). Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation in HgTe wells, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, whose authors are not credited in this entry. The 3D topological insulator discovery (Moore-Balents, Fu-Kane-Mele, Hasan, Cava) lies outside the credited names, which may be an issue. A 3-person prize of Kane, Mele, Molenkamp is plausible.
assessment.maturity: Mature: more than fifteen years of confirmation, many independent experiments and widespread use. Recognition is timely or somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Omission of Bernevig, Zhang, König and the 3D topological-insulator pioneers from the credited set.
Overlap with B010, which proposes a different mix of names for the same area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices implement clean, tunable Hubbard-type models and allow quantum simulation of many-body phenomena, such as the superfluid-Mott transition, with single-site resolution later. This has had major influence on how many-body quantum physics is studied and is conceptually very clear and deep.
assessment.attribution: Zoller with Jaksch and collaborators supplied the theoretical proposal, Greiner with Bloch and Hänsch carried out the superfluid-Mott experiment and Bloch led the lattice programme. Cirac's contributions and the role of Hänsch's group make this a difficult selection among four credited names, and Greiner's relative role against Bloch is not obvious to me.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by independent groups, with a mature quantum-simulation field. Timing is reasonable, though the cold-atom field has been recognised several times already (BEC 2001, cooling 1997, frequency comb 2005).
uncertainties: Choice of three among Bloch, Cirac, Greiner and Zoller; the proposed trio is my best judgement.
Overlap with Zoller and Cirac in B034 and B036, which could split credit across prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks with magic-wavelength trapping reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, enabling tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. The invention is original, concrete and measurably important in precision metrology.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept in 2001-2003 and Ye's group demonstrated extreme precision and many-body clock physics. A two-person prize is clean. Credit for the Sr lattice clock demonstration and the role of Lemonde, Takamoto and others may need care.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed, with several independent labs reaching comparable accuracy. A redefinition of the second is still pending, but scientific impact is already clear, so timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as sufficiently distinct from earlier time and frequency prizes (Ramsey, Hall and Hänsch, Wineland).
Detailed priority between Katori's proposal and early experiments is from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and entanglement-based E91) is a foundational application of quantum mechanics to information security, tied directly to Bell tests and quantum information science. The concepts are original and of long-lasting influence, and experiments reach commercial and satellite scale.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard published BB84, Ekert independently proposed the entanglement-based protocol in 1991. A three-person split is possible, although whether Ekert's contribution should be treated on equal terms with BB84 is debated. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is not among the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Mature in concept and widely demonstrated, though practical security against side-channel attacks remains an active engineering topic. The 2022 prize on Bell tests partly overlaps conceptually. Recognition is arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Attribution weighting of BB84 against E91 and the Wiesner precursor.
Whether physics rather than computer science or engineering is the appropriate home for part of the work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error-correcting codes and fault-tolerance concepts demonstrate that large-scale quantum computation is possible in principle despite decoherence. This is the conceptual foundation for the entire quantum-computing roadmap, including the surface code, which is very close to my work. Experimental demonstrations below threshold have recently appeared.
assessment.attribution: Shor (first code, 1995) and Steane (independent CSS code, 1996) and Kitaev (topological codes and fault tolerance) are credible, but Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Preskill and others also made decisive contributions that are not available in the credited names, so the three-person limit is uncomfortable.
assessment.maturity: Experimental support is still emerging; below-threshold logical qubits are recent, so the physical vindication is not yet mature. Recognition may be somewhat premature but is highly relevant.
uncertainties: Large number of key contributors compared with the three-person limit.
Experimental maturity is incomplete, and I am relying on memory for recent milestone details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory provides a nonperturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons, and in combination with first-principles methods it has become a standard tool for studying Mott transitions and correlated materials. It is a clear conceptual and computational advance.
assessment.attribution: Georges and Kotliar developed the mapping onto the Anderson impurity model in 1992 and Vollhardt, with Metzner, introduced the infinite-dimensional limit in 1989. Metzner is not among the credited names, which weakens the attribution picture; the three names given are credible in terms of effect on the field.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with wide use over three decades. The central physics is robust, though the method is an approximation and its limits in low dimensions are known.
uncertainties: Omission of Walter Metzner from the credited names.
Whether a theory-method prize fits the committee's preference for discoveries with direct experimental confirmation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum control of mechanical motion (ground-state cooling, quantum states of macroscopic mechanical oscillators, optomechanical entanglement) extends quantum physics to massive objects and ties into superconducting-circuit and sensing technologies. It is a significant and coherent set of results.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and Martinis demonstrated a mechanical resonator in its quantum ground state in 2010, Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer pioneered cavity optomechanics. Teufel, Lehnert, Painter and Schwab also contributed decisively and are not in the credited set, so attribution is contested.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by multiple groups with continued progress. The field is somewhat younger and applications are still evolving, so recognition could be considered a little early.
uncertainties: Multiple groups with overlapping claims on first ground-state cooling and quantum-regime demonstrations.
Proximity to the 2025 prize topic on macroscopic quantum behaviour in circuits.
